ch3n3.title: The door in the snow

questions.q: The Rat and the Mole are lost, but they try hard to stay brave. How do we know?

options.text: They pretend every new tree is an old friend, to keep each other cheerful.
options.why: Clue: they go on "pretending with invincible cheerfulness that they recognized an old friend in every fresh tree". Pretending to be cheerful is how you stay brave.

options.text: They sing loud marching songs so that the animals in the wood can hear them.
options.why: Clue check: look through the first few paragraphs. Is there any singing at all?

options.text: The Rat tells the Mole he knows exactly where the path home is from here.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 1 the Rat says "I don't exactly know where we are". He is honest, not boastful.

options.text: they run fast
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and the idea slips past too. Clue check: paragraph 2 says they walk "holding on to each other". Nobody runs.

questions.q: They are *hopelessly at sea*. What does that mean?

options.text: They are completely lost and have no idea which way to go.
options.why: Clue: the same paragraph says there is "no end to this wood, and no beginning" and "no way out". At sea means totally lost.

options.text: They have walked so far that they can see the sea ahead of them.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 3 says the trees are "thicker and more like each other than ever". They are deep in a wood, nowhere near a beach.

options.text: The snow has melted into water and they are wading right through it.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 3 says the snow is "getting so deep". It is piling up, not melting.

options.text: totally lost
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Can you spot the option that says it properly?

questions.q: How does the Rat know the Mole's cut was not made by a branch?

options.text: The cut is so clean and neat that something sharp and metal did it.
options.why: Clue: "It's a very clean cut... Looks as if it was made by a sharp edge of something in metal." A branch would make a messy scrape.

options.text: The Rat saw the whole thing happen, and there wasn't a single tree nearby.
options.why: Clue check: the Rat only works it out afterwards, by "examining it again attentively". He is looking at the cut, not remembering.

options.text: The Rat thinks the Mole is fibbing about falling over, just to get attention.
options.why: Clue check: the Rat says "Poor old Mole!" and ties up the leg. He believes him completely.

options.text: clean sharp cut
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: The Mole says "never mind what done it". What does the Rat dig up a little later that proves the Mole should have minded?

options.text: A door-scraper, which means somebody's front door must be very close by.
options.why: Clue: the Mole finds "A door-scraper!" That is the sharp metal thing that cut him, and door-scrapers sit outside front doors.

options.text: A sharp branch, which proves that the Mole really did just trip on a stump.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 10 the Rat says the cut "was never done by a branch or a stump".

options.text: An old lost knife, which means there are robbers hiding somewhere in the wood.
options.why: Clue check: read paragraph 17 again. The Mole names the thing he sees. Is it a knife?

options.text: a door-mat
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and it's not quite right either. Clue check: the door-mat turns up later, in paragraph 21, and a soft mat can't cut a leg.

questions.q: The Rat cries out *in despair at his obtuseness*. What is the Rat so fed up about?

options.text: The Mole can't see what the clues mean, and the Rat can't bear it.
options.why: Clue: just before this, the Mole says the scraper only means someone "VERY careless" left it there. He can't see what it really means, and that is what obtuseness is.

options.text: The Rat is upset because the Mole's poor leg is hurt so very badly.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 10 says it is "a very clean cut" and the Rat has already tied it up. That's not what is upsetting him now.

options.text: The Rat has given up every hope of ever getting out of the wood.
options.why: Clue check: in the very same sentence the Rat shouts "come and scrape!" Someone who had given up wouldn't keep digging.

options.text: Mole not getting it
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: Why does the Mole start digging too, even though he thinks the whole thing is silly?

options.text: He digs to keep the Rat happy, as he thinks the Rat has gone a bit silly.
options.why: Clue: he scrapes "more to oblige the Rat than for any other reason", because he thinks his friend is "getting light-headed".

options.text: He suddenly understands all the clues and wants to be first to find the door.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 28 calls him the "hitherto incredulous Mole". Right up until the door appears, he still doesn't believe it.

options.text: He hopes to find a second door-scraper so he can take one home for himself.
options.why: Clue check: the Mole thinks door-scrapers are "domestic litter". He doesn't want another one!

options.text: to keep warm
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and the idea slips past too. Clue check: paragraph 27 gives his real reason, and it's about the Rat.

questions.q: At the start of tonight the Rat says he doesn't know where they are. What has changed by the time they read the little brass plate?

options.text: They know they are at Mr. Badger's house, and he can take them in.
options.why: Clue: the plate says "MR. BADGER." Now they know exactly where they are, and it's a friend's front door.

options.text: They know they are back at the river bank, right outside the Rat's home.
options.why: Clue check: the door is "in the side of what had seemed to be a snow-bank" in the wood. There's no river anywhere.

options.text: They know the Mole's own house is close by, under the snowy hummocks.
options.why: Clue check: read the name on the brass plate in paragraph 30. Whose name is it?

options.text: Badger's front door
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: The Mole cries out *in penitence*. How is he feeling?

options.text: He is sorry he laughed at the Rat's clues and called them rubbish.
options.why: Clue: he says "you're a wonder!" and "I see it all now!" Penitence means feeling sorry. He had called the mat "domestic litter" and now he knows he was wrong.

options.text: He is cross that the Rat was the one who found the door, and not him.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 31 the Mole says "If I only had your head, Ratty". He is full of praise, not cross.

options.text: He is frightened that Mr. Badger will be very angry at being woken up.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 31 the Mole falls over "from sheer surprise and delight". Delight isn't fright.

options.text: very cold
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and the idea slips past too. Clue check: penitence is about a feeling inside, not the weather. Look at what the Mole says to the Rat.

questions.q: Which word best describes the Rat tonight, and what is your proof?

options.text: Clever: he works out from a neat cut and a mat that a door is near.
options.why: Clue: the Mole says it himself: "You argued it out, step by step, in that wise head of yours."

options.text: Lazy: he sits down on a log and lets the Mole do all of the digging.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 27 says the Rat attacked the snow-bank "with ardour" and dug "with fury". That's the opposite of lazy.

options.text: Careless: he doesn't even look at the Mole's leg after he falls over.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 8 says the Rat goes "down on his knees to look" and ties it up with his handkerchief.

options.text: Timid: he is too scared to ring the bell, so the Mole has to do it.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 33 the Rat "attacked the door with his stick" while the Mole rang. Nobody was scared.

questions.q: Where does tonight's bit of the story end, and how is the Mole feeling?

options.text: Swinging on the bell-pull at Badger's door, full of hope and excitement.
options.why: Clue: the Mole "clutched it and swung there, both feet well off the ground", and far away they hear the bell. Help might be coming!

options.text: Tucked up in a warm bed at Badger's house, safe after a very long night.
options.why: Clue check: the last paragraph is still outside the door. Nobody has opened it yet.

options.text: Still lost in the snow, cross that the Rat keeps dancing silly jigs about.
options.why: Clue check: by the end they've found the door, and the Mole thinks the Rat is "a wonder".

options.text: fast asleep
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and the idea slips past too. Clue check: in the last paragraph the Mole is swinging off his feet on a bell-pull. Is that asleep?

hints: Nobody comes for ages, so the Mole keeps ringing until slow footsteps shuffle up to the door.
A grumpy voice tells them to go away, but when it hears the Rat's name it lets them in at once.
Nobody is home, so the Rat finds a key under the door-mat and they let themselves in.
The bell wakes the whole Wild Wood, so the Rat keeps the faces away with his pistols until the door opens.
